```{r setup-knitr, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

## Apply a theme to every panel

{gratia}'s `draw()` combines the individual plots for model terms into one
figure using {patchwork}. The `&` operator applies a {ggplot2} theme to every
panel, so you can style them together.

Load the plotting packages and simulate 400 observations. The covariates are
independent and range from zero to one.
Three have nonlinear effects on the mean response; `x3` has no true effect.
Independent Gaussian noise adds variation with standard deviation 2.

```{r setup-data}
library("gratia")
load_mgcv()
library("ggplot2")
library("dplyr")
library("patchwork")

# simulate data
n <- 400
eg1 <- data_sim("eg1", n = n, seed = 1)
```

Fit a Gaussian GAM with one smooth for each covariate. REML selects the
smoothness; we will reuse this fitted model throughout the plotting examples.

```{r setup-chunk}
# fit model
m <- gam(y ~ s(x0) + s(x1) + s(x2) + s(x3),
  data = eg1, method = "REML")
```

Save the default figure as `p` so we can apply different styles to the same
fitted smooths.

```{r draw-eg1-}
p <- draw(m)
p
```

Adding a theme with `+` changes only the last panel in this combined figure.
The following example makes that behaviour visible: only the final smooth
receives the white background from `theme_bw()`.

```{r draw-eg1-wrong-theme}
p + theme_bw()
```

Use `&` to apply the same theme to all four panels.

```{r draw-eg1-right-theme}
p & theme_bw()
```

## Change curve colours, intervals and other plot components

gratia has theme settings for smooth curves, interval ribbons, residual
points and reference lines. Here we make every smooth navy, give it a thicker
line and use a pale navy interval ribbon.

```{r native-component-theme}
p & theme(
  geom.gratia.smooth = element_geom(colour = "navy", linewidth = 0.8),
  geom.gratia.interval = element_geom(fill = "navy"),
  gratia.alpha.interval = 0.15
)
```

Use `geom.gratia.partial.residual` for partial residuals,
`geom.gratia.diagnostic.point` for diagnostic points, and
`geom.gratia.reference` for reference lines. Opacity uses numeric settings
such as `gratia.alpha.interval` and `gratia.alpha.diagnostic.point`.
More specific settings, such as `geom.gratia.smooth.interval`, override
the general interval setting. See `?gratia_theme_get` for the component list.

Use `gratia_theme_set()` when you want subsequent gratia figures to share a
style. Save its return value so you can restore the previous settings after
drawing the figure.

```{r native-package-theme}
old_theme <- gratia_theme_set(theme(gratia.alpha.interval = 0.1))
draw(m)
gratia_theme_set(old_theme)
```

These settings affect gratia plots created afterwards. For a temporary change,
you can instead use `withr::with_options()` with the `gratia.plot.theme`
option. If you have older code using arguments such as `smooth_col` or
`ci_alpha`, replace those arguments with theme settings as shown above.

Common replacements for deprecated arguments are:

| Previous argument | Theme setting |
|:--|:--|
| `smooth_col` | `geom.gratia.smooth = element_geom(colour = ...)` |
| `ci_col`, `ci_alpha` | `geom.gratia.interval = element_geom(fill = ...)`, `gratia.alpha.interval` |
| `resid_col` | `geom.gratia.partial.residual = element_geom(colour = ...)` |
| `contour_col` | `geom.gratia.contour = element_geom(colour = ...)` |
| `point_col`, `point_alpha` in diagnostics | `geom.gratia.diagnostic.point = element_geom(colour = ...)`, `gratia.alpha.diagnostic.point` |
| `line_col` in diagnostics | `geom.gratia.diagnostic.reference = element_geom(colour = ...)` |
| `colour`, `alpha` in smooth samples | `geom.gratia.sample = element_geom(colour = ...)`, `gratia.alpha.sample` |
| `ci_3d_col`, `ci_3d_alpha` | `geom.gratia.surface.interval = element_geom(fill = ...)`, `gratia.alpha.surface.interval` |
| `alpha`, `linewidth` in chain diagnostics | `gratia.alpha.chain`, `geom.gratia.chain = element_geom(linewidth = ...)` |

Use `geom.gratia.effect` for parametric curves and `geom.gratia.derivative`
for derivatives. Rootograms have separate `rootogram.bar`,
`rootogram.fitted`, `rootogram.reference` and `rootogram.warning` elements.
MRF interval lines use `geom.gratia.smooth.interval`, independently of the
points controlled by `geom.gratia.smooth`. Diagnostic boxplots use
`geom.gratia.diagnostic.boxplot`.

## Laying out labels, legends and colour bars

Long labels can overlap when several plots share a figure. Use
`draw_label_control()` to choose wrapping widths and guide layouts, then pass
the result as `label_control` to `draw()` or `assemble()`. The configuration
works across drawing methods.

For a categorical axis, wrapping breaks long labels into lines and `n_dodge`
staggers labels across rows. We simulate observations in three fishing
categories so we can illustrate both options. The response combines a curved
effect of day, a difference between categories and independent Gaussian noise
of standard deviation 0.3.

```{r label-layout-data}
set.seed(430)
fishing <- data.frame(
  day = runif(150, 0, 300),
  angler_type = factor(rep(c("Boat (guided)", "Boat (unguided)", "Shore"), 50))
)
fishing$y <- sin(fishing$day / 60) +
  c(0, -0.8, -0.3)[as.integer(fishing$angler_type)] + rnorm(150, sd = 0.3)
```

Fit a GAM with a smooth effect of day and a parametric effect of fishing
category. Wrap the fishing-category labels and stagger them over two rows.

```{r label-layout-axes}
fishing_model <- gam(y ~ angler_type + s(day, k = 8),
  data = fishing, method = "REML")
axis_layout <- draw_label_control(axes = list(wrap = 12, n_dodge = 2))
draw(fishing_model, label_control = axis_layout, ncol = 2)
```

Legends have their own wrapping width and can arrange their entries into rows
or columns. Compare the fitted day smooth with one that has a smaller basis
and no smoothing penalty (`fx = TRUE`). The smaller basis limits how much the
curve can bend. Use descriptive labels for the two fits and wrap the entries
in a single legend column.

```{r label-layout-legend}
simple_fishing <- gam(y ~ angler_type + s(day, k = 3, fx = TRUE),
  data = fishing, method = "REML")
comparison <- compare_smooths(fishing_model, simple_fishing, n = 50)
comparison$.model <- factor(comparison$.model,
  levels = c("fishing_model", "simple_fishing"),
  labels = c("More flexible curve across the season", "Less flexible curve across the season"))
legend_layout <- draw_label_control(
  legend = list(wrap = 22, title_wrap = 18, ncol = 1)
)
draw(comparison, label_control = legend_layout)
```

Colour bars can wrap their titles, rotate their tick labels, and change their
displayed dimensions. The following pairwise concurvity plot shows how closely
each smooth can be approximated by another smooth in the four-smooth model.
The fill scale supplies the title and the label control wraps it and sets the
bar height. Use the scale to set the palette, breaks and numeric labels.

```{r label-layout-colourbar}
bar_layout <- draw_label_control(
  axes = list(wrap = 15),
  colourbar = list(title_wrap = 18, height = grid::unit(35, "mm"))
)
draw(model_concurvity(m, pairwise = TRUE),
  continuous_colour = scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Concurvity between model terms"),
  label_control = bar_layout)
```

Wrapping happens after scale labels have been formatted, preserving custom
labels, mathematical expressions and explicit line breaks. Use
`axes = list(title_wrap = ...)` to wrap axis titles. Wrapping and staggering
tick labels applies only to discrete axes.

## Use a different palette for groups

Grouped curves and ribbons use the Okabe–Ito palette for up to nine groups,
and a hue palette for more than nine. Supply a palette function to both the
colour and fill theme settings to keep each model's curve and interval the
same colour. Here we use Paul Tol's bright palette for the model comparison.

```{r native-tol-palette}
tol <- gratia_palette("tol_bright")
draw(comparison) &
  theme(palette.colour.discrete = tol, palette.fill.discrete = tol)
```

Paul Tol choices include bright and vibrant (7 colours), muted (9),
dark (11), and banded schemes (12, 16 or 20). The dark palette is designed
for a white background. Choose a palette with enough colours for all your
groups. A request for more colours than the palette provides gives an error.
See `?gratia_palette` for available names.

Continuous palettes can also be changed through
`palette.fill.continuous` and `palette.colour.continuous`. Existing scale
arguments still accept complete scales when custom transformations,
breaks or guides are needed.

## Combining individual plots produced by `draw()`

Each `draw()` result is already a combined figure, even if it contains only
one smooth. When combining several results, specify their layout explicitly.
First, here is the error that can occur when those dimensions are omitted.

```{r draw-multiple-patchworks, error = TRUE, fig.show = "hide"}
p1 <- draw(m, select = "s(x0)")
p2 <- draw(m, select = "s(x1)")
p3 <- draw(m, select = "s(x2)")
p1 + p2 + p3
```

Add `plot_layout(ncol = 3)` to place the three results in one row.

```{r draw-multiple-patchworks-layout}
p1 + p2 + p3 + plot_layout(ncol = 3)
```

When all smooths come from the same model, select them in one `draw()` call
and supply `ncol` directly.

```{r draw-multiple-patchworks-draw}
draw(m, select = c("s(x0)", "s(x1)", "s(x2)"), ncol = 3)
```

The explicit layout is useful when the plots come from different models or
need to be arranged with other ggplot2 figures.

## Grouping factor smooths and showing their intervals

`grouped` selects which factor smooth types share a plot. Choose any of
`"factor-by"`, `"sz"`, and `"fs"`. Types omitted from the vector are drawn
separately for each level, or each evaluated combination of levels for `sz`
terms with several factors. `show_ci` independently selects which of these
types show interval ribbons. These controls apply to curves with one
continuous covariate; ordinary smooths and surface plots retain their displays.

The defaults, `grouped = c("sz", "fs")` and
`show_ci = c("factor-by", "sz")`, retain the existing grouping and interval
visibility. Use `FALSE` to select none. Separate curves use the usual
univariate styling: a black fitted line and a translucent black interval.
We simulate `x2` between zero and one and use `fac` to identify three groups.
The response combines a different curve of `x2` in each group with independent
Gaussian noise of standard deviation 2. We then fit three ways of representing
these relationships. A factor-by smooth fits a curve for each group;
an `sz` smooth represents group deviations from a shared curve; an `fs`
smooth estimates group curves whose penalties share smoothing parameters.

```{r factor-plot-data}
factor_data <- data_sim("eg4", n = 400, seed = 244)
```

Fit the three representations to the same data so we can compare how their
group curves are displayed. Each model uses REML to select its smoothing
parameters.

```{r factor-plot-models}
m_by <- gam(y ~ fac + s(x2, by = fac), data = factor_data, method = "REML")
m_sz <- gam(y ~ s(x2) + s(x2, fac, bs = "sz"),
  data = factor_data, method = "REML")
m_fs <- gam(y ~ s(x2, fac, bs = "fs"),
  data = factor_data, method = "REML")
```

Overlay the factor-by curves with intervals:

```{r factor-by-grouped}
draw(m_by, grouped = "factor-by", parametric = FALSE)
```

Separate the `sz` deviations and hide their intervals. The ordinary smooth
retains its interval:

```{r sz-separate-no-intervals}
draw(m_sz, grouped = FALSE, show_ci = "factor-by")
```

`fs` terms represent a fitted curve for each factor level. Separate those
curves and include their intervals with:

```{r fs-separate-intervals}
draw(m_fs, grouped = FALSE, show_ci = "fs")
```

The same controls work with saved estimates. Grouping the curves or hiding
their intervals leaves the saved estimates and interval limits intact. Here
we draw each group deviation separately and omit its interval ribbon.

```{r factor-saved-estimates}
sz_estimates <- smooth_estimates(m_sz)
draw(sz_estimates, grouped = FALSE, show_ci = FALSE)
```

Ordered-factor `by` smooths use `"factor-by"` too. In the following model,
`s(x2)` is the reference smooth and the ordered-factor terms describe
deviations for the other levels. Grouping overlays only those deviations;
the reference smooth remains a separate plot. No smooth is created for the
ordered factor's first level, and the displayed deviations do not have the
reference smooth added to them.

```{r ordered-factor-grouping}
factor_data$ordered_fac <- ordered(factor_data$fac)
m_ordered <- gam(y ~ fac + s(x2) + s(x2, by = ordered_fac),
  data = factor_data, method = "REML")
draw(m_ordered, grouped = "factor-by", parametric = FALSE)
```

`grouped_by` is deprecated. Replace `grouped_by = TRUE` with
`grouped = c("factor-by", "sz", "fs")`; replace `grouped_by = FALSE` with
`grouped = c("sz", "fs")`. During migration, an explicit `grouped_by`
updates only `"factor-by"` membership in `grouped`.

## Drawing surfaces in 3D

With the optional {ggcube} package installed, use `surface = "3d"` to view a
two-dimensional smooth as a surface. First simulate a nonlinear
response over two covariates with independent Gaussian noise of standard
deviation 0.2, so the surface's peaks remain visible above the noise.

```{r surface-3d-data, eval = requireNamespace("ggcube", quietly = TRUE)}
eg2 <- data_sim("eg2", n = 400, scale = 0.2, seed = 2)
```

Fit a tensor product smooth with 15 basis functions per covariate to allow
enough flexibility for the nonlinear surface; REML selects its smoothness.
Then draw the smooth's contribution to the linear predictor. `n_2d = 50`
evaluates the surface on a 50-by-50 grid, and `yaw` controls the viewing angle.

```{r surface-3d, eval = requireNamespace("ggcube", quietly = TRUE)}
m_surface <- gam(y ~ te(x, z, k = c(15, 15)),
  data = eg2, method = "REML")
draw(m_surface, surface = "3d", n_2d = 50,
  surface_3d = list(yaw = 45, persp = FALSE))
```

Pass camera settings through `surface_3d`, which forwards them to
`ggcube::coord_3d()`. For example, `persp = FALSE` uses a parallel projection
so distant parts of the surface do not appear smaller.

The covariates form the two horizontal axes and the partial effect forms the
vertical axis. Use `surface = "tile"` for a flat rectangular display or the default
`surface = "raster"` for a compact image. These choices display the same
estimated effect.

## Build a plot from smooth estimates and partial residuals

Themes control the appearance of plots returned by `draw()`. To choose
different layers or map additional variables to aesthetics, build a plot
from the estimates returned by gratia.

First evaluate the fitted smooths with `smooth_estimates()` and add pointwise
interval limits with `add_confint()`. Each row contains a value of the
covariate, the estimated smooth at that value and its interval limits.

```{r custom-plot-eval-and-add-confint}
# evaluate the smooths
sm <- smooth_estimates(m) |>
  add_confint()
sm
```

To add partial residual points, use `add_partial_residuals()` on the fitting
data. In this Gaussian model with an identity link, a partial residual for a
smooth is the observation minus the fitted intercept and the contributions of
the other terms. These are the points shown by `draw(m, residuals = TRUE)`.

```{r custom-plot-add-partial-resids}
# add partial residuals to data
eg1 <- eg1 |>
  add_partial_residuals(m)
```

The new columns use the smooth labels as names, such as `s(x0)` and `s(x1)`.
Inspect the names so we can select the column matching the smooth to plot.

```{r custom-plot-names}
names(eg1)
```

Plot the smooth for `x2` using five layers:

1. a rug plot of the observed values of `x2`,
2. the credible interval around the estimated smooth,
3. the partial residuals as a point layer,
4. the estimated smooth as a line layer,
5. an axis label and title.

```{r custom-plot-sx2}
p_sx2 <- sm |>
  filter(.smooth == "s(x2)") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_rug(aes(x = x2),
    data = eg1,
    sides = "b", length = grid::unit(0.02, "npc")
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .lower_ci, ymax = .upper_ci, x = x2),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(x = x2, y = `s(x2)`),
    data = eg1, size = 1.5, colour = "steelblue3"
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(x = x2, y = .estimate), linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(y = "Partial effect", title = "s(x2)")
p_sx2
```


We prepare equivalent plots for the other three smooths to combine with this
one below. Their construction repeats the same steps, so the code is hidden.

```{r custom-plot-other-smooths, echo = FALSE}
p_sx0 <- sm |>
  filter(.smooth == "s(x0)") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_rug(aes(x = x0),
    data = eg1,
    sides = "b", length = grid::unit(0.02, "npc")
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .lower_ci, ymax = .upper_ci, x = x0),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(x = x0, y = `s(x0)`),
    data = eg1, size = 1.5, colour = "steelblue3"
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(x = x0, y = .estimate), linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(y = "Partial effect", title = "s(x0)")

p_sx1 <- sm |>
  filter(.smooth == "s(x1)") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_rug(aes(x = x1),
    data = eg1,
    sides = "b", length = grid::unit(0.02, "npc")
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .lower_ci, ymax = .upper_ci, x = x1),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(x = x1, y = `s(x1)`),
    data = eg1, size = 1.5, colour = "steelblue3"
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(x = x1, y = .estimate), linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(y = "Partial effect", title = "s(x1)")

p_sx3 <- sm |>
  filter(.smooth == "s(x3)") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_rug(aes(x = x3),
    data = eg1,
    sides = "b", length = grid::unit(0.02, "npc")
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .lower_ci, ymax = .upper_ci, x = x3),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(x = x3, y = `s(x3)`),
    data = eg1, size = 1.5, colour = "steelblue3"
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(x = x3, y = .estimate), linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(y = "Partial effect", title = "s(x3)")
```

Combine the four plots and set `ncol = 2` to arrange them in two columns.

```{r custom-plot-final}
p_sx0 + p_sx1 + p_sx2 + p_sx3 + plot_layout(ncol = 2)
```

## Colour partial residuals by another variable

A custom plot can show information beyond the variables in the fitted
smooth. To demonstrate grouping, create an arbitrary four-level factor and
use it to colour the residual points. This factor is unrelated to the
simulated response and is used only to demonstrate the colour mapping.

```{r add-factor-to-data}
set.seed(12)
eg1 <- eg1 |>
  mutate(fac = sample(letters[1:4], n(), replace = TRUE))
```

Build the curve and interval first, then add the partial residuals with
`fac` mapped to colour. Adding the points last keeps them visible above the
interval ribbon.

```{r plot-partial-resids-with-colours-by-fac}
plt <- sm |>
  filter(.smooth == "s(x2)") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_rug(aes(x = x2),
    data = eg1,
    sides = "b", length = grid::unit(0.02, "npc")
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .lower_ci, ymax = .upper_ci, x = x2),
    alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(x = x2, y = .estimate), linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(y = "Partial effect", title = "s(x2)")

plt +
  geom_point(
    aes(
      x = x2, y = `s(x2)`,
      colour = fac
    ),
    data = eg1, size = 1.5
  )
```

To look for patterns involving another fitted covariate, map `x1` to point
colour and size. We remove the fixed point size so it can vary with `x1`.

```{r plot-partial-resids-with-colours-by-x1}
plt +
  geom_point(
    aes(
      x = x2, y = `s(x2)`,
      colour = x1, size = x1
    ),
    data = eg1, alpha = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "plasma")
```

If points of the same colour consistently fall above or below the fitted
curve, residuals may still vary with `x1`. The
[model diagnostics article](model-checking.html) shows how to check that
pattern by plotting residuals directly against a covariate.
